summary: This informational document establishes definitions and measurement techniques for benchmarking data center network equipment, and introduces new terminology for performance tests of switches. It sets the shared vocabulary used by the companion methodology document, RFC 8239.

plainLanguage.summary: Before you can race fairly, everyone needs to agree on what words like finish line and lap mean. This agrees on the words for testing data center network gear.

questions: how to define data center network performance tests
what is data center benchmarking terminology
subtitle: Shared vocabulary for benchmarking data center switches: latency, jitter, line rate, buffers, incast and goodput.

tldr.problem: Older benchmarks focus on maximum throughput and latency, and do not represent the bursty, many-to-one traffic that data center switches really see.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC defines terms and measurement units for latency (FILO, FIFO, LILO, LIFO), jitter, line rate, buffer size, microbursts, incast and goodput, and says which must be used.
tldr.outcome: It is the terminology prerequisite for the test methodology in RFC 8239.

today: RFC 8238 is an Informational RFC published in August 2017, and the metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. Its test methods are in RFC 8239.

sections.title: Why Data Center Switches Need New Terms
sections.content:
Data center traffic is not uniform. It can run east-west (server to server) or north-south (outside to server), be bursty, and include many-to-one, many-to-many or one-to-many flows, with a mix of UDP and TCP. Earlier benchmarks such as RFC 1242, RFC 2544 and RFC 2889 measure theoretical maximum throughput and latency but do not represent these real patterns.

RFC 8238 describes typical devices as having 48 or more ports, speeds up to 100 GB/s per port, and buffers in the MB range. It defines the terms, and the test methods live in RFC 8239. Each term follows a fixed format: Definition, Discussion and Measurement Units.
sections.plainLanguage: Switches in a data center get crowds of messages all at once. The old tests only checked how fast one message could go, so we need new words for the crowd.

sections.title: Latency and Jitter
sections.content:
Latency is the time a frame takes to transit the device under test (DUT). The RFC names four ways to measure it, by which bit of the input and output frame starts and stops the clock.

  • FILO (first bit in, last bit out) MUST be used, because it includes the serialization delay and covers both store-and-forward and cut-through devices.
  • FIFO (first bit in, first bit out) MAY be used for applications that can work on the first bytes of a frame.
  • LILO (last in, last out) is also listed.
  • LIFO (last bit in, first bit out) MUST NOT be used, because it subtracts the frame's own latency and can give negative values on cut-through switches.

The event combination used MUST always be reported. This replaces the latency definition in RFC 1242 for data center switch benchmarking.

Jitter means delay variation. The mandatory form is Packet Delay Variation (PDV) from RFC 5481: each packet's delay minus the minimum delay, summarized as a range (Max - Min) or a high percentile such as the 99th. Inter-Packet Delay Variation MAY be used to see whether a stream has become bursty. Results are in seconds.
sections.plainLanguage: Latency is how long a parcel spends inside the sorting machine. The RFC says to start the stopwatch when the first bit goes in and stop it when the last bit comes out, so big parcels count properly.

sections.title: Calibration and Line Rate
sections.content:
Calibration of the physical layer means recording everything that adds latency to the test: traffic generator type, line cards, transceivers, cable type and length, and software versions. Cables SHOULD ideally be the same type and length from the same vendor. The report MUST say whether cable latency was subtracted and give the traffic generator's accuracy, usually within about 20 ns.

Line rate is the maximum rate of frames of a given size at the transmit clock. Two connected Ethernet interfaces never have exactly the same clock, and the standards allow +/- 100 PPM. Example from the RFC for 1 GB Ethernet with 64-byte frames: 1,000,000,000 / 672 = 1,488,095.2 frames per second.

Because a test set running even 1 PPM faster than the switch will slowly fill buffers and cause drops, line rate SHOULD be measured at 99.98% with a 0 PPM adjustment, or at 100% with a -100 PPM adjustment.
sections.plainLanguage: Two clocks never tick at exactly the same speed. If the sender ticks a hair faster, the receiver slowly gets swamped, so testers send slightly under full speed.

sections.title: Buffers, Microbursts and Incast
sections.content:
The RFC defines several buffer measures: buffer size (total frame-buffering memory), port buffer size, maximum port buffer size (which for switch-on-chip designs adds the shared pool a port may use) and maximum DUT buffer size. Each must be given with the MTU and the CoS or DSCP value used. Its example reports 18 MB for 1518-byte frames. A larger buffer is not necessarily better and can cause bufferbloat.

A burst is a fixed number of packets sent over a percentage of line rate. A microburst is a burst that causes drops without sustained congestion on the link. Its intensity is a percentage between 1 and 100.

Incast is the many-to-one or many-to-many pattern. Frames have synchronous arrival times if any of their bits overlap on the DUT, and the percentage of synchronization is the level of that overlap. A test MUST report the number of ingress and egress ports and a non-null percentage of synchronization.
sections.plainLanguage: Buffers are waiting rooms inside the switch. When many kids arrive at one door at the same moment, that is incast, and the waiting room fills up fast.

sections.title: Goodput
sections.content:
Goodput is application-level throughput: bits per unit of time forwarded to the correct destination interface of the DUT, minus any retransmitted bits. It is a variant of the definition in RFC 2647. For TCP applications even a small loss can sharply reduce it, so goodput SHOULD be measured.

The formula is G = (S/F) x V, where S is the payload bytes without packet or TCP headers, F is the frame size and V is the media speed in bytes per second. The RFC's example is a TCP transfer on 10 GB/s media: 1460 payload bytes in a 1526-byte Ethernet frame gives 9.567 Gbit/s. Reports should also note the TCP stack, OS versions and NIC firmware and model.
sections.plainLanguage: Goodput counts only the useful part of what arrived, like the candy inside the wrapper and not the wrapper itself.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content: Benchmarking here is limited to technology characterization with controlled stimuli in a laboratory with dedicated address space. The test topology MUST NOT be connected to devices that could forward test traffic into a production network or misroute it to the test management network. Testing is black-box, and special capabilities SHOULD NOT exist in the DUT only for benchmarking. The RFC requests no IANA actions.
sections.plainLanguage: Run tests in a closed practice yard so the test traffic never leaks onto real roads.

items.label: First in, last out
items.desc: MUST be used; includes serialization delay.

items.label: First in, first out
items.desc: MAY be used for applications that can use the first bits.

items.label: Last in, last out
items.desc: Starts at the last input bit, ends at the last output bit.

items.label: Last in, first out
items.desc: MUST NOT be used; subtracts the frame's own latency.
